extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of poetics; poets, dramatists, and critics interested in classical theory of tragedy and poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for composing and judging poetry and especially tragedy according to Aristotle’s Poetics: what imitation is, the elements of tragedy, requirements for plot and character, diction, and practical rules for the tragic poet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation (mimesis) as the principle of the arts
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Imitation’ (mimesis) is the common principle of the arts of poetry, music, dancing, painting, and sculpture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These arts are distinguished according to three aspects — the medium, the objects, and the manner of imitation — and the treatment of imitation is the basis for defining poetic genres and assessing artistic practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium of imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Medium of Imitation is Rhythm, Language, and ‘Harmony’ (or Melody), taken singly or combined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different arts employ different media (e.g., flute uses harmony and rhythm, dancing uses rhythm alone, language alone may be used in prose or verse). The chosen medium shapes the form and effects of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of imitation (higher or lower types)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Objects of Imitation: Higher or lower types are represented in all the imitative arts. In Poetry this is the basis of the distinction between Tragedy and Comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representation of men as better, worse, or as they are distinguishes genres; epic and tragic poets often portray elevated types, comic poets lower or degraded types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of imitation (form/genre)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry may be in form either dramatic narrative, pure narrative (including lyric poetry), or pure drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manner of imitation (narration vs. presentation of action) is a core classificatory and evaluative criterion — e.g., drama represents action directly and is often called 'drama' for that reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origins and psychological basis of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry arises from two causes — the instinct of Imitation and the instinct of Harmony and Rhythm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This locates poetic practice in natural human instincts (learning by imitation and pleasure in rhythm), implying that good poetry appeals to these faculties; historical divergence (epic vs. lampoon) follows from individual aptitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tragedy and its six elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition of Tragedy. Six elements in Tragedy: three external — Scenic Presentment (opsis), Lyrical Song (melopoiia), Diction (lexis); three internal — Plot (mythos), Character (ethos), and Thought (dianoia). Plot is of primary importance; Character and Thought come next.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or evaluating tragedy, check for the presence and quality of these six elements, giving primacy to plot coherence and design, then to characterisation and intellectual content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot, or the representation of the action, is of primary importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A tragedy’s success depends chiefly on the plot's organization and effect; character and thought are secondary but essential supports to a well-constructed plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot must be a Whole and of adequate magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: The Plot must be a Whole, complete in itself, and of adequate magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A plot should form a unified, self-contained action of suitable length and scope so that the piece feels complete; avoid fragments or sprawling plots lacking coherent closure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Plot (unity of action)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Plot must be a Unity. Unity of Plot consists not in Unity of Hero, but in Unity of Action. The parts must be organically connected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether incidents are causally and organically linked to a single action or purpose; scenes or subplots that do not contribute to the central action violate unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic truth vs. historic truth — probable/necessary sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic Unity can be attained only by the observance of Poetic as distinct from Historic Truth; for Poetry is an expression of the Universal, History of the Particular. The rule of probable or necessary sequence is applied to the incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept departures from literal factual chronology when they better express universal truths; incidents should follow one another by probability or necessity rather than by mere chronological accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of the Inevitable and the Unexpected
rubrics_metrics.description: The best Tragic effects depend on the combination of the Inevitable and the Unexpected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-crafted plot yields outcomes that feel both necessary (inevitable) and startling (unexpected); avoid outcomes that are either wholly predictable or wholly arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple and Complex plots; reversal, recognition, and tragic incident
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions of Simple (without reversal/recognition) and Complex (with reversal — peripeteia, recognition — anagnorisis, and tragic or disastrous incident — pathos) plots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex plots use structural devices (reversal, recognition) to produce emotional and intellectual effects; assess whether such devices are credibly integrated and enhance unity and catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative parts of Tragedy (prologue, episode, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ‘quantitative parts’ of Tragedy are defined — Prologue, Episode, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although some passages are interpolated, these structural divisions (prologue, episodes, choral odes) serve constituent roles; assess how each part contributes to the whole and the movement of the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic action: change of fortune and appropriate hero
rubrics_metrics.description: What constitutes Tragic Action: The change of fortune and the character of the hero as requisite to an ideal Tragedy. The unhappy ending more truly tragic than the ‘poetic justice’ preferred by popular audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragic action should involve a significant reversal in the hero’s fortune suited to the character’s moral stature; prefer serious, meaningful catastrophe over contrived moral neatness for the sake of tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pity and Fear must spring from the Plot itself
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic emotions of pity and fear should spring out of the Plot itself. To produce them by Scenery or Spectacular effect is entirely against the spirit of Tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotional responses should be elicited by the internal logic and incidents of the drama, not by external spectacle or sensational stage effects (an anti-pattern).

rubrics_metrics.name: Character as manifestation of moral purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The element of Character (as the manifestation of moral purpose) in Tragedy. Requisites of ethical portraiture. The rule of necessity or probability applicable to Character as to Plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should act consistently with their moral purpose and probability; their actions must be necessary or plausible given their established character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deus ex machina and out-of-place resolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The ‘Deus ex Machina’ is criticized as a passage out of place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid resolutions that rescue the plot by implausible or external contrivances; endings should emerge from the plot’s internal causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character idealisation
rubrics_metrics.description: How Character is idealised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters in poetry are often presented in an idealised manner appropriate to the poetic form; judge whether idealisation serves the work's moral and artistic aims without negating probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical rule — vivid sympathy via embodiment and rehearsal
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical rules for the Tragic Poet: (1) To place the scene before his eyes, and to act the parts himself in order to enter into vivid sympathy with the dramatis personae.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should imaginatively embody and 'act' scenes during composition to achieve convincing dramatic presence and empathetic characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical rule — sketch the bare outline first
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical rules for the Tragic Poet: (2) To sketch the bare outline of the action before proceeding to fill in the episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan the unified action and its major turns before writing detailed scenes or speeches to preserve unity and avoid extraneous material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Care with complication and dénouement
rubrics_metrics.description: Further rules: (1) To be careful about the Complication (skope) and Denouement (lusis) of the Plot; especially the Dénouement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct complications and resolutions so they grow inevitably from preceding incidents; the dénouement must be the natural outcome of the plot rather than an afterthought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unite varied forms of poetic excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: Further rules: (2) To unite, if possible, ‘varied forms of poetic excellence.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where feasible, harmonize different poetic strengths (musical elements, diction, plot, character) so the work attains multiplicity of excellence without fragmentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overloading tragedy with epic details
rubrics_metrics.description: Further rules: (3) Not to overcharge a Tragedy with details appropriate to Epic Poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain genre-appropriate scale and detail; avoid epic-length digressions or minutiae that distract from dramatic immediacy and unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make choral odes organic
rubrics_metrics.description: Further rules: (4) To make the Choral Odes—like the Dialogue—an organic part of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choral elements should contribute to plot, theme, or mood rather than functioning as decorative or disconnected interludes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought and its expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought (dianoia), or the Intellectual element, and Diction in Tragedy: Thought may be expressed either by the dramatic speeches—composed according to the rules of Rhetoric—or through the dramatic incidents, which speak for themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether ideas are conveyed effectively through speeches or action; overly rhetorical exposition may be less effective than embodied thought in incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction and Poetic Diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction, or Language in general: an analysis of parts of speech and other grammatical details; Poetic Diction: The words and modes of speech admissible in Poetry, including Metaphor in particular. How Poetry combines elevation of language with perspicuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate language for both elevated tone and clarity; poetic devices (metaphor, elevated diction) are appropriate but must not obscure meaning or undermines dramatic truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic vs Tragedy — shared unity and distinguishing features
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic Poetry agrees with Tragedy in Unity of Action. Points of difference are enumerated — namely, (1) the length of the poem; (2) the metre; (3) the art of imparting a plausible air to incredible fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing or adapting forms, consider these differences: epic scale and epic conventions differ from tragedy’s focused action and immediate dramatic requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy defined by imitation of lower types (the ludicrous)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy is an imitation of characters of a lower type — the Ludicrous being merely a subdivision of the ugly; it consists in some defect or ugliness which is not painful or destructive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy’s evaluative frame rests on representing defects that provoke laughter without invoking real pain; judge whether comic elements adhere to this principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification principle — imitation, not metre, defines the poet
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when verse combines different metres or consists of one kind, it is imitation that makes the poet, not the metre. The verse alone does not entitle an author to the name 'poet' — imitation does.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not evaluate a poet or poetic work solely on formal metrical features; consider the imitative content and how it shapes the poetic identity and effect.
